targets.authors: Shevlin, M.; McBride, O.; Murphy, J.; Miller, J.G.; Hartman, T.K.; Levita, L.; Mason, L.; Martinez, A.P.; McKay, R.; Stocks, T.V.A.; et al.
targets.title: Anxiety, depression, traumatic stress and COVID-19-related anxiety in the UK general population during the COVID-19 pandemic.
targets.evidence_quote: In a second part of the analysis, we replicated the approach by Shevlin et al. [19].
targets.outcome_quote: Summarizing, these results are in line with those of the UK study about anxiety, depression, and traumatic stress [19]. The UK and Italian data identify factors associated with worst psychological health: being a woman, younger age, having children, preexisting health issues of self or someone close, and the moderate to high perceived risk of contracting COVID-19 within one month. Unlike Italy, in the UK lower household incomes and having (had) the COVID-19 were associated with worst psychological health outcomes.
targets.outcome_reasoning: The authors explicitly identify matching risk factors and contrasting findings; the first sentence concerns these results rather than an overall verdict on the whole replication.

targets.title: COVID-19-related anxiety predicts somatic symptoms in the UK population.
targets.evidence_quote: In particular in this paper we focus on anxiety, depression, and stress related to COVID-19 and on the comparison with the same measurements from the first wave of the UK C19PRC study [19,20].
targets.outcome_quote: The PHQ-15 subscales and the total score were positively and significantly correlated with COVID-19 anxiety, as well as with GAD-7 total score. These correlations are in line with results from the first wave of the UK study [20].
targets.outcome_reasoning: Explicit agreement on the association of COVID-19 anxiety with somatic symptoms; more linear shape does not negate the supported substantive association.
